transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in to see me today?

Hello, Dr. Smith. Well, I guess I came in because... well, even on my better days lately, I just can't shake this feeling I've been having. It's the people at my church and the ladies in my walking club. I just know they're watching me, and they keep putting these little hidden messages about me in the Sunday bulletin, or slipping things about me into what they say when we're together. 

The walking club usually meets on Tuesdays at the park, right near the old bandstand. They painted that bandstand a bright blue last summer, which was just a terrible choice if you ask me. It completely clashes with the oak trees. My late husband used to say you should never paint outdoor wood, you should only ever stain it. He stained our back deck every three years like clockwork. He was so meticulous about things like that. We used to sit out there and drink iced tea... but yes, I just don't understand why they're putting those messages in the bulletin about me. I've been going to that parish for thirty years.
How long have you been noticing these hidden messages and feeling that people are watching you—has this been going on for weeks, months, or longer?

Well, let me think... it's been about eleven months now. Yes, eleven months of the messages, and the voices, and just having so much trouble keeping my thoughts straight. It started right around the time my sister Carol bought her new car. It's a Honda, a silver one. I told her silver shows every little speck of dirt, but she wouldn't listen. She never listens. When we were little, she insisted on cutting her own bangs and looked absolutely ridiculous for our cousin's wedding. Aunt Martha was furious. Aunt Martha made the best potato salad, though—she always put a little bit of dill in it. I try to do that now, but it never tastes quite the same. But yes, eleven months of all this going on.
Have you or your family noticed any recent changes in your memory, such as forgetting recent conversations, appointments, or getting confused about where you are or what day it is?

Oh, no, my memory is just fine. I haven't been forgetting anything like that. I always know exactly what day it is, and I keep track of all my appointments on my kitchen calendar. It's one of those beautiful Thomas Kinkade ones with the little lit-up cottages. My niece gets me a new one every single Christmas. We usually have a big glazed ham for Christmas dinner, though this past year it was terribly dry. I told Carol she left it in the oven too long, but you know how she is, she just brushed me off. She was too busy fussing over that centerpiece she made. She spray-painted all these pinecones gold. I think gold is a bit tacky for a dining table, honestly. Silver or crystal is much more elegant. My mother had this gorgeous crystal punch bowl we used to bring out for the holidays... it caught the light just perfectly. But no, I haven't noticed any confusion or anything.

Over these past eleven months, have you also gone through stretches of feeling extremely sad, hopeless, or low in energy, or times when you felt unusually elated, full of energy, or needed much less sleep than usual?

Well, the sadness... yes, that's been there even longer. I'd say the deep sadness, the feeling guilty all the time, and just not caring about my walking club or anything else... that's been going on for about a year and two months now. It started right around the time the grocery store down the street changed their layout. 

They moved the bakery section all the way to the back, which makes no sense at all. You want to smell the fresh bread right when you walk in, don't you? That's how the old A&P used to do it when I was a girl. My mother would send me down with a quarter to get a loaf of rye, and Mr. Henderson—he was the baker—would always give me a free cookie. He had a glass eye, you know. He lost his real one in the war, though he never liked to talk about it. He just wore this little eye patch sometimes when the glass one bothered him. But yes, the sadness and having no energy at all, that's been about fourteen months. I haven't felt elated or anything like that, just so very low.
During this past year, have there been any stretches of time when you were not feeling sad or low, but you still noticed the hidden messages or heard the voices?

Well, let me think about that... yes, there was. There was a spell of several weeks, maybe a few months back, where I actually felt a bit lighter. I was getting dressed every morning, putting on real clothes instead of my bathrobe, and eating a bit better. I wasn't feeling quite so weighed down by everything. But those messages and the voices, they didn't stop. I still kept hearing my name being called out when I was alone in the house, and I was absolutely sure the people at church were hinting about me during the announcements. 

Speaking of church, Pastor Greg has been talking about painting the sanctuary for ages now. He wants to do it a pale yellow, but Mrs. Higgins from the choir is dead set against it. She says yellow washes out the stained glass windows. Her husband, Earl, used to do all the handyman work around the church before his arthritis got bad. He built those lovely wooden racks for the hymnals. They used a nice cherry wood... or maybe it was oak? I can never tell the difference, really. My father loved oak. He built a whole dining set out of oak when I was little, but it was so heavy we could barely move the chairs to sweep under the table. But yes, even when I wasn't feeling quite so miserable, the voices and the hints were still there.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports persistent psychotic symptoms (persecutory delusions about church members and walking club, auditory hallucinations of her name being called) lasting 11 months, concurrent with a major depressive episode (depressed mood, guilt, anhedonia, low energy) lasting 14 months. Critically, she confirms a distinct period of several weeks where depressive symptoms remitted (improved grooming, appetite, functioning) yet the delusions and hallucinations persisted independently. This temporal pattern—mood episode overlapping with psychotic symptoms, plus a discrete period of psychotic symptoms without mood disturbance—meets criteria for Schizoaffective Disorder, Depressive Type (F25.1), rather than Major Depressive Disorder with psychotic features (which would require psychosis only during mood episodes) or primary psychotic disorder (which would not require the mood episode overlap). Cognitive complaints were denied, making neurocognitive disorder unlikely.
